webTitle: Legal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’

fields.headline: Legal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’
fields.trailText: Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’
fields.bodyText: A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US. Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups. These legal outfits and like-minded allies have won key lawsuits on election issues, plus litigation thwarting Trump’s moves to end birthright citizenship and a $1.8bn slush fund that could have paid money to allies including January 6 rioters he deemed were unjustly charged. Since Trump returned to power, for instance, Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center have jointly filed lawsuits against Trump’s 2025 and 2026 executive orders on voting, challenging their constitutionality to set new voting rules that by law are run by the states. Key legal briefs they filed together include an August one on behalf of several voting rights groups and local officials in two states to block Trump’s March 2026 executive order that would restrict voting by mail and authorize the US Postal Service to implement rules to that end. Other groups that have accelerated their legal challenges to Trump’s moves to thwart voting rights and expand his executive powers in other ways, include the Brennan Center for Justice, Democracy Forward, members of the Democratic Attorneys General Association and the Washington Litigation Group. Last month, for instance, 24 Democratic attorneys general and other plaintiffs filed suit to block USPS from moving forward with rules to curb mail voting and in late August won a temporary 14-day restraining order from federal judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts. In response, the justice department’s solicitor general, John Sauer, on Thursday appealed to the supreme court to lift the injunction, arguing in heated words that the freeze would create “serious, irreparable harm on the federal government, the states themselves, and the voting public”. On 4 September Talwani made her injunction permanent, writing that implementing Trump’s order so close to the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail”. She also stressed that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.” Sauer on 6 September responded with another emergency appeal to the high court urging it permit the new USPS rules to go into effect, claiming that it “does not seize control of states’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail”. In a related twist, a detailed whistleblower complaint that the Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut released last week alleged that the USPS had been proceeding with a “secretive, rushed” effort to implement Trump’s order that could lead to “catastrophic failure” with this year’s mail-in voting. About 50 million Americans, the majority of whom are Democrats, vote by mail, according to reports. With the elections about two months away, the legal groups are stepping up efforts to thwart “self-serving attempts to take over the midterms”, said a former justice department lawyer, which experts fear may create chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters. Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at the Campaign Legal Center, told the Guardian: “The CLC and the DDF have worked closely together on two ongoing lawsuits challenging the president’s unlawful voting executive orders that attempt to dictate election rules. We’ve teamed up in the supreme court on a brief filed by former state and federal judges, including noted conservative judges, that emphasized just how unlawful and dangerous the president’s efforts to dictate election rules are.” Baldwin, who spent 14 years in the justice department’s civil rights division, said the CLC and the DDF have also “worked together in federal cases filed in Oregon and California to make sure that the DoJ isn’t able to seize voters’ sensitive data by making false claims about non-citizen voting. In cases around the country, the Campaign Legal Center is pushing back on the DoJ’s lawless efforts to vacuum up and aggregate sensitive data to create a national voter file of some sort.” Further, former ambassador Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund, which he co-founded in 2023, told the Guardian that since its inception the DDF has been involved in more than 300 legal cases and matters in three primary areas: elections, the rule of law and anti-corruption. Eisen said the group, whose board boasts former federal judge and conservative stalwart J Michael Luttig and liberal-leaning ex-federal judge Nancy Gertner, likes to work in conjunction on cases with other ideologically diverse and non-partisan groups like the CLC and the WLG because “they both have strong bipartisan credibility. It’s a big-tent approach we’ve taken with our election work.” Eisen said Luttig and Gertner were instrumental in helping recruit dozens of former judges with bipartisan credentials to file amicus briefs on multiple matters including an August one to the supreme court opposing Trump’s 2026 executive order to curb mail voting. For its part, the WLG this summer hired about half a dozen new lawyers to handle election-related litigation. “As the midterms approach with growing concerns about potential federal interference in elections, we’ve brought on more attorneys to be even more prepared to litigate sensitive matters under acute time pressure,” said James Pearce, a principal with the WLG. Elsewhere, Sophia Lin Lakin, who leads the ACLU Voting Rights Project, said the group had been “pushing back” on administration efforts to seize personal voting data from states, and said the ACLU had been involved in 26 of 30 legal challenges to the administration on the issue. To date, the administration has lost 23 cases where rulings have been made. Critics say Trump, the justice department, the USPS and the Department of Homeland Security seem to be laying the groundwork for further attacks on the nation’s election rules, citing Trump’s false claims about election fraud and his radical plans to change voting rules. In July in a televised speech, Trump falsely portrayed the nation’s voting system as riddled with fraud and condemned voting by mail and non-citizen voting. “Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” Trump claimed without evidence, even though he voted twice by mail this year. Trump, who continues to blame voting fraud for his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, also charged that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically minuscule, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s fixation on noncitizen voting is belied by a database from the rightwing Heritage Foundation that only cites 100 cases over a quarter-century. But according to documents reviewed by the New York Times, hundreds of DHS agents have been engaged in a hunt to find noncitizens among registered voters. The chief of the DHS has said ICE agents could be sent to polling places “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant”. The justice department has helped to amplify Trump’s bogus election claims with legal threats and actions. In July, Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the department’s civil rights division, wrote to officials in 50 states warning that “any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state’s [voter list] or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability”. In August, the justice department announced plans to send a larger-than-usual contingent of 1,000 lawyers to monitor voting nationwide, raising concerns that such large efforts could lead to voter intimidation. And in a harbinger of coming legal fights, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform last month that the justice department’s Ed Martin, a key election denialist in charge of pardons, was leaving to handle election-related litigation. Former justice department lawyers say administration threats to voting rights make opposition from legal advocates crucial. Stacey Young, a lawyer who left the department at the start of 2025 after 18 years to found Justice Connection, a group of more than 3,000 ex-justice department lawyers and other alumni, denounced Trump’s moves “to interfere” with elections. “The constitution makes clear that the president has no authority over the administration of our elections, but that hasn’t stopped this president, or those he put in power at the justice department, from trying to interfere,” Young said in a statement. “We’re taking these threats seriously and leveraging our collective strengths to protect election integrity, which is key to maintaining a functioning democracy.” Justice Connection is working with experts in its alumni network to engage with the media, Congress and the public to highlight the justice department’s traditional role in election security and ensuring compliance with federal voting laws. Other justice department alumni agree that opposition to Trump’s election agenda is critical. “These organizations are doing critical work in protecting the ability of people to vote and make their voices heard – a cornerstone of democracy,” said Michael Bromwich, a former Department of Justice inspector general. “The full-out assault on democracy must be addressed through the courts because Congress has proven itself unwilling and unable to check the undemocratic steps taken by the administration.” Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney for eastern Michigan who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, said: “Large law firms sent armies of young attorneys to our nation’s airports to represent individuals caught up in Trump’s travel ban. That is not happening any more because of the ‘deals’ they negotiated with the Trump administration in his second term to support his pet causes. “Thank goodness for groups like the Democracy Defenders Fund, which are attracting top legal talent and challenging some of Trump’s lawless activities. Their work is protecting the rights of all Americans.” Further, Nick Brown, Washington state’s attorney general, who chairs an election protection group for the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said it had teamed up with some legal advocacy groups such as the Brennan Center, States United and the DDF to hold “strategy sessions” to prepare for potential disruptive moves by the Trump administration in the November elections. Brown also attacked the administration’s appeal to the supreme court to move forward with Trump’s executive order on voting by mail, despite Judge Talwani’s strong concerns and litigation against it by Democratic attorneys general. He said: “As the court said, states’ compliance with this illegal order would be ‘practically impossible’ before the November elections given the unprecedented demands it would put on state and local elections officials. The chaos that would cause is exactly what Trump wants. That’s why we continue to fight for a fair and properly administered election.” Baldwin too raised strong concerns about the justice department’s push to get the supreme court to issue a ruling that would expedite Trump’s executive order on voting by mail. She said: “The DoJ’s slapdash effort at getting the supreme court’s blessing to turn the USPS into a gatekeeper for mail would be a farce, if it didn’t put our fundamental right to vote in the crosshairs. Given the importance of what is at stake, the DoJ’s continued efforts are nothing more than an attempt to foist chaos on the electoral process. But they will fail.” Other lawyers engaged in key election legal battles and other litigation voice optimism they will prevail. Tianna Mays, the legal director of the DDF, said: “The Trump administration has declared war on the rule of law, yet our democratic guardrails are still holding. We refuse to stand by idly while this administration flouts the constitution and attempts to eviscerate our institutions.” This article was updated on 7 September 2026 to reflect that members of the Democratic Attorneys General Association have filed suit, not the Daga itself.

webTitle: Republican midterm convention will be ‘Trumpist pageantry’ – at the party’s own risk

fields.headline: Republican midterm convention will be ‘Trumpist pageantry’ – at the party’s own risk
fields.trailText: A historically unpopular president will take centre stage as the party seeks to sway voters with an unprecedented event
fields.bodyText: It seemed like a good idea at the time. In December 1978, Jimmy Carter, a US president besieged by inflation and energy crises, watched as thousands of Democrats descended on Memphis, Tennessee, for a rare midterm convention. “It was wild,” recalls Elaine Kamarck, who attended as a 28-year-old working for the Democratic National Committee. “It became a forum for Ted Kennedy to informally announce his opposition to President Carter. There was a lot of hostility to the president there. The Democrats have sworn ever since never to do anything this stupid again.” The 1978 convention took place after midterm elections in which Democrats suffered losses but still maintained control of the House of Representatives and Senate. The party also held midterm conventions in 1974 and 1982. Kamarck, who later served in the Bill Clinton administration, adds: “The Democratic party has never thought of doing this again and, whenever it has, people like me say, ‘No, are you absolutely crazy?’” Republicans, however, did not get the memo. This week in Dallas, Texas, the party will stage a midterm convention for the first time. Donald Trump will deliver a keynote address on Wednesday and closing remarks on Thursday. Other speakers include Vice-President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr and the president’s son Donald Trump Jr. The convention has been billed as a “primetime showcase” to boost morale, nationalise congressional elections and galvanise Republican voters. But success is far from guaranteed. The made-for-TV spectacle clashes directly with the two opening games of the American football season. A Politico website survey of more than 70 Republican candidates and members found 45 who either do not plan to go to Dallas or are still thinking about it. Some cited prior commitments while others balked at the $25,000 price of attending. Unlike conventions in a presidential election year, delegates will not be making party rules or drawing up a policy platform. “This is essentially a Trump rally that they’re calling a midterm convention,” said Kamarck, now a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington. “They’re trying to get enthusiasm among their base because that’s what they need for November. Basically, this is a Trump show.” That ambition probably made sense when the midterm convention was first mooted. Republican voters are historically slow to turn out when Trump is not on the ballot. By putting himself on the marquee, the president – who defied the odds to win the White House in 2024 – is hoping to narrow the enthusiasm gap. Among those hoping for a boost from Trump in Texas is Senate candidate Ken Paxton, whose history of scandals – including an affair and securities-fraud indictment – could prove costly against the Democratic rising star James Talarico. But now it appears the plan could backfire. Trump’s approval rating is ‌at 33%, the lowest point of his political career, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll last week. Democrats seem more fired up about the midterms with 46% describing themselves as “very enthusiastic” about voting in November, compared with 31% of Republicans. Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, warns that building a midterm convention around a failing president is tantamount to “political suicide”. “It is an incredibly risky strategy for any Republican at this point to hitch his wagon to Donald Trump,” she explained. “On every issue that Trump was once strong on he is underwater, from the economy to immigration.” Setmayer, co-founder of the political action committee the Seneca Project, added: “The idea that he’s going to excite people is flawed at this point, given the polling numbers in Donald Trump’s own constituency. They’re not inspired and this vanity convention is not going to change that with 60 days to go to the election. If anything, it’s going to remind people of how dissatisfied they are under Donald Trump’s second term.” There are further signs that the president could be more of a curse than a blessing. Some candidates are quietly scrubbing his likeness from their websites in a tactical retreat. In Texas, candidate Carlos De La Cruz replaced “TRUMP CONSERVATIVE” with “PROVEN CONSERVATIVE” on his homepage, erasing a line about being “ready to be President Trump’s wingman in Congress” for a platitude about “servant leaders”. In Kentucky, Ralph Alvarado pivoted to “INDEPENDENT LEADERSHIP”. In Nevada, Martin O’Donnell, a music composer best known for his work on the Halo video game series, no longer features his Trump endorsement photo on his website. In south Texas, Eric Flores replaced “SUPPORT PRESIDENT TRUMP’S AGENDA” with “LOWER THE COST OF LIVING”. In Alaska, Nick Begich edited his homepage to a simple: “We have delivered for Alaska.” Elsewhere, candidates are actively breaking ranks. The Wisconsin congressman and gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany publicly rebuked Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as “Lake America” and opposed importing cheaper ground beef. The Michigan congressman Tom Barrett is campaigning on his votes to limit Trump’s war in Iran, highlighting his support for the War Powers Resolution. Trump, however, appears unmoved and indifferent. Allan Lichtman, a history professor at American University in Washington, said: “He doesn’t care about any of these other candidates. He only cares about two things when it comes to the midterms: one, that he won’t be investigated and two, that he can get his appointments through the Senate. He demands loyalty for everyone else and gives loyalty to no one.” A Republican source said at least 100 members of Congress were expected to attend the convention and more than 20,000 tickets had been distributed, ensuring a packed arena. The source denied that Trump would dominate proceedings, insisting that the convention would aim to “energise our base, inform folks there is an election and highlight the contrast between what Republicans are offering – which is a secure border, safe communities, cutting taxes, giving Americans more freedom – and what the Democrats are offering, which is reopening the borders, repealing the tax cuts, investigating, obstructing, impeaching President Trump and not having an agenda beyond that”. The source also rejected reports that Republican candidates were distancing themselves from the president, saying: “We have Republican candidates across the country who want the president in their districts. You see it with Mike Lawler, who’s one of two Republicans left in Congress still in a district that Kamala Harris won in 2024. I believe the president has campaigned for him in his district twice. Mike Lawler does a very good job of embracing the president’s policies. He deviates on certain issues when needed.” The convention schedule will also aim to steady the ship. The first night will include segments focused on tax cuts, healthcare affordability, the border, trade and domestic manufacturing, with appearances by “workers and everyday Americans”. The second will highlight families benefiting from policies like no taxes on tips, overtime and social security, as well as overseas prisoners who have been released, border security, efforts to lower prescription drug costs and a tribute to the slain rightwing activist Charlie Kirk. The convention will also try to appeal to the “Maha” – or Make America healthy again – wing of the party, with a segment targeting corporate influence in the treatment of chronic diseases. And it will mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks with families of first responders. But the program makes no mention of any programming related to foreign policy or the deeply unpopular war in Iran. Lichtman observed: “People aren’t buying what they have to say, which is things are getting better, it’s the golden age, prices are coming down, we’re winning the Iranian war, our immigration policy is great. They’re not gonna buy it just because it’s a convention. Plus, as we know, Trump always goes off script and that’s never helpful to his party.” But Republicans do seem to believe they have an ace up their sleeves. Trump and his allies are expected to go in hard on a theme pointing to the primary election successes of democratic socialists and casting Democrats as godless communists and Marxists who pose an existential threat to the American way of life. Charlie Sykes, a conservative broadcaster and author of How the Right Lost Its Mind, said: “The midterms will either be a referendum on Donald Trump, in which case they will be disastrous for the Republicans, or Republicans will hope that they can make this a referendum on the radicalism of Democrats, so I’m guessing that will be a major theme. “The big question is, who is going to be paying any attention to this? Who is going to be watching this other than the hardcore base, the already convinced? I have a very hard time imagining independent voters tuning in to see the Trumpist pageantry.” But commentators believe that the convention, with its potential to draw primetime TV viewers and generate viral clips, could make a difference in the margins. Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, said: “It might increase Maga’s turnout. That’s the only positive in this thing potentially for Republicans. “It’s not going to change any minds but it might convince the Maga people, ‘Well, I don’t normally vote when our hero is not on the ballot but if this is what Donald wants me to do, I’m going to pitch in and help.’ But it’s not going to help that much.” The midterm convention could have an intriguing subplot. Along with Vance, the Texas senator Ted Cruz and other potential 2028 presidential contenders will be in attendance for what could be an early audition. Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, said: “Anybody who looks in the mirror and sees a president looking back at him or her, if those people are speakers, it will be a chance for them to make an impression.” Such aspirants would be wise to tread carefully, however, since Trump is not likely to cede the limelight willingly. Sykes added: “It is a Trump-a-palooza and once again Donald Trump insists on being – what was the old phrase about Teddy Roosevelt? – the bride at every wedding and the corpse at every funeral. “He wants to make the midterms all about himself despite the fact that he’s reaching the Nixon line in terms of polling unpopularity. It’s very much on brand except that right now, with every day we get closer to the midterms, Trump’s narcissism becomes a greater challenge to Republicans who want to survive what looks like a blue wave.”
